articles.fullContent: Theoretical astrophysics · a whole field · audited by machine I had AI read my entire field. 158,059 papers and 554,670 citations. Every paper with full text screened, 659 of the most important recomputed and checked, and every verified error followed through the papers that cite it. This is the map, and what it says about whether science corrects itself. WhyErrors that nobody fixed I spent five years in this field doing my PhD at Caltech, and a few months of that went to errors in the literature that were already known. The equations my code was built on came from Bishop, Gómez, Lehner, Maharaj & Winicour, “High-powered gravitational news” (1997), the paper the subfield's characteristic codes descend from. People knew it had mistakes. The fixes were scattered through some 10,000 lines of intersecting email threads that contradicted each other, and the paper itself was never corrected. The best I could do was correct the record in my own papers: an appendix setting out the full set of equations, made consistent, and a parenthetical “with a sign error in s3 corrected” for anyone reading closely. That is the limit of human literature review. Mine was not deep: my three thesis papers cite fewer than a hundred papers between them, in a field of tens of thousands. Nobody re-derives every equation they cite, referees check one paper once, and nobody is paid to go back and fix the original. So every student who builds on a broken paper pays the same tax, one at a time, and the correction lives in somebody's inbox. A machine can read the whole field, recompute it, and follow each error to every paper that copied it. So I had one do it. It found errors in my own papers too. The mapEvery dot is a paper Height is time: the 1960s at the bottom, this year at the top. Each faint line is a citation. The bright dots are the papers everything else leans on, ranked the way Google ranked the early web. The seed is TAPIR, Caltech's theoretical astrophysics group, where I did my PhD: 4,093 papers by its 326 members since 2004. Add every paper they cite and every paper that cites them and you get 158,059 papers joined by 554,670 citations. The 49,301 drawn here are the ones tied to TAPIR at least three times over. A century in ten secondsWatch it grow The map holds 499 papers from the 1970s, 2,035 from the 1990s and 18,976 from the 2010s. The old layers are the survivors, the papers people working today still cite. Everything else from 1975 has already been forgotten, right or wrong. Most of what this field knows was written in the last twenty years, by people who are still around to answer email. Hold that thought. SubfieldsA subfield is a column Nobody told the layout what numerical relativity is. Papers that cite each other pull together, so a subfield shows up as a column: the same few dozen people writing about the same problem year after year, each layer standing on the last. There are 32 columns, from fast radio bursts to the Milky Way's halo. One columnNumerical relativity Solving Einstein's equations on a computer until two black holes merge. 278 papers in this column, 71 of them TAPIR's, busiest in 2010. Every subfield has a page: the questions it is organised around and whether each is open, contested or settled, who wrote the central papers and where, how fast it publishes, and which of its errors we traced. Each open question also carries a flag for what today's AI could do about it. Of 155, a model judged 8 answerable now from data and codes that already exist, 119 ones AI would speed up, and 28 stuck waiting on a telescope or a detector. articles.fullContent: 1Duke University2UIUC3Harvard University arXiv Code TL;DR – We introduce Energy-Based Reasoners (EBRs), reasoning models that learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. Its value scores candidate predictions without requiring an external verifier, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a natural signal for stopping. With only 1.8M parameters, EBRs achieve 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345× less inference compute than the next-best model. On N-Queens and Graph Coloring, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. Abstract Looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning. By repeatedly iterating a recurrent block, looped models can scale their effective depth and enable multi-step reasoning in latent space. However, existing looped models are not inherently guided by an explicit measure of progress, making it difficult to determine when to stop looping and how to improve upon the current state. To enable this, we introduce Energy-Based Reasoners (EBRs), which learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. The energy scores latent states, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a signal for stopping. To train EBRs effectively, we further introduce exploration-based training to discover additional modes and to better shape the energy landscape over a broader set of states. Across four algorithmic reasoning benchmarks, EBRs match or outperform prior recurrent reasoning models, achieving 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345× less inference compute than the next-best model and maintaining comparable training compute. On all multi-solution benchmarks, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage of distinct valid solutions while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. These results suggest that energy-based models are a promising approach for strong reasoning performance. Why Energy? Existing looped reasoners update their latent state without any explicit assessment of it. An EBR learns an energy function that guides refinement, stopping and selection. Score. The energy rates the compatibility between the reasoning state and the initial board . Lower means better compatibility. Refine. The gradient turns the score into an improvement direction. Stop. The state becomes stationary once the gradient is small, so the gradient acts as a stopping criterion. Select. Among multiple candidate solutions, we pick the one with the lowest energy. Correct solutions settle at low-energy stationary states. Energy, gradient norm and step size during descent on Sudoku-Extreme. Correct trajectories settle at low energy with small gradients, while wrong ones keep moving. Test-Time Scaling Running more descent steps refines each answer further, and running more trajectories gives the energy more candidates to choose the lowest-energy one from. EBRs reach EqR's best accuracy with 7× fewer iterations (left) and 43× fewer samples (right). GRAM and TRM from GRAM's paper; EqR from its released checkpoint. Mean ± SD over three seeds. Adaptive Stopping Each trajectory stops once its energy gradient falls below a threshold, so easy puzzles finish in a few steps and hard ones keep going. articles.fullContent: Posted on May 26, 2026 This is the traffic to All About Berlin, the website that I run since 2017, and live from since 2020. After 7 years of growth, it has lost 70% 75% of its traffic to Google AI Overviews. When you Googled something, you used to get a link to my website. Now you get a page of ads, then an AI-generated answer trained on my content, then finally a link to my website. This has a devastating impact on traffic. What it means to be first on Google It’s hard to fund my work with only a quarter of my audience. Soon, I will need another way to pay my rent. Instead of writing new guides, I already spend my days preparing for that future. It’s not just about the money. I have poured 8 years of my life into making something good and useful. Strangers’ faces light up when they learn that I run All About Berlin. Local and federal government offices refer people to my guides. The Berlin immigration office uses my data about themselves. It inspired two government portals and a few similar websites in other cities. If my work just get mixed into an AI-generated answer, I lose my voice and my audience. My carefully chosen words lose their meaning. No one shakes my hand and buys me a beer. No one tells me how their citizenship application went. This is not an isolated case. Many website owners have reached out in private to commiserate. Some have paywalled their work. Others have given up and moved on. They keep the websites online, but they no longer update them. It’s just not worth it. It will get worse. Last week, Google has made two announcements: AI-generated answers will replace search results entirely, and they have ads in them.1 This is the future of the internet. No websites, just a chat box with ads. I don’t know where All About Berlin fits in that future. This was also discussed on Mastodon, Hacker News, LinkedIn and Twitter. If you are affected, reach out. Let me know how you are doing. You are not going through this alone. articles.fullContent: I was inspired to create my first Fibonacci LED piece after seeing this video by Jim Bumgardner in 2015. I credit him for starting my Fibonacci obsession.Fast forward to 2026. I’ve made dozens of Fibonacci designs. Recently, I saw this brilliant post by Nick Pisarro explaining the use of the golden angle in creating his beautiful Halo Pixel. It got me thinking about how to explain the techniques I use.Every Fibonacci board I make, from the tiny One Inch Fibonacci64 to the Fibonacci1024, puts its LEDs on a Fermat spiral, the same pattern as the seeds in a sunflower. It’s different from the “Fibonacci spiral” drawn from squares, which is a single curve. The Fibonacci step shows where the name comes from. The rules Start at the center. Then repeat: Step out a little. Add an LED. Turn 137.508°. Every LED on every¹ Fibonacci board is placed by those rules. LED n sits n × 137.508° around from the first, and about √n out from the center. The next two steps explain those two numbers. ¹ There are exceptions to the √n rule, of course, like Fibonacci64 Flower and Fibonacci256 Expanding. The golden angle Any simple fraction of a turn makes spokes. At 90° (a quarter turn), every 4th LED lands on the same line. 120° makes 3 spokes, and 135° (3/8 of a turn) makes 8. At 137° the LEDs still bunch into arms with gaps between them. 137.5° is exactly 55/144 of a turn, so the edge starts to crowd. The golden angle, 360° ÷ φ² ≈ 137.508°, can’t be written as a fraction at all, so the LEDs never line up. The animation measures how close the two nearest of 600 LEDs get, as a percentage of the spacing in a perfect honeycomb. angle closest two LEDs 90° 4% 135° 9% 137° 55% 137.5° 82% 137.508° (golden) 87% The golden angle isn’t the only angle that scores well, though. Other “noble” angles, like 99.5°, come close. The golden angle is the one that’s furthest from every fraction. Angles past 180° just mirror these: 222.492° (360° − 137.508°) makes the same spiral, flipped. That’s why you’ll sometimes see the golden angle given as about 222.5°. √n spacing With the angle set, the next question is how far each LED steps out from the center. Each cell in the animation is the part of the board that’s closer to its LED than to any other. If every step out is the same size, the edge has far more room than the middle but gets no more LEDs, so the LEDs end up crowded together in the middle and far apart at the edge. The biggest cell is about 150 times the size of the smallest. A disc’s area grows with the square of its radius, so the steps out have to shrink as you go. Stepping out by √n gives every LED the same share of the board, and neighboring LEDs end up evenly spaced. The biggest cell is then only 1.3 times the smallest. If the steps shrink faster than that, it flips, with the LEDs far apart in the middle and crowded at the edge. With equal area for every LED, the pixel density is the same all the way across the board. You can always add one more A square grid only looks tidy at square numbers, rings only when every ring is full, and a hex grid only at 7, 19, 37, 61… The faint outlines in the animation show the spots each layout still needs to fill before it looks right again. The spiral is an even, round disc at every count, and adding an LED never moves any of the others. The Fibonacci32, Fibonacci64, Fibonacci128, Fibonacci256, Fibonacci512 and Fibonacci1024 all use the same layout, with differently sized LEDs and different spacings, each stopped at a different count. Where the Fibonacci numbers come from Look closely at any of the boards and you’ll see spiral arms. Connect every 3rd LED and you get 3 arms, because the golden angle is close to 1/3 of a turn. Every 5th LED makes 5 arms curving the other way, every 8th makes 8, and so on. Each of those fractions (2/5, 3/8, 5/13, 8/21…) is a little closer to the golden angle than the last, so each set of arms is a little straighter. articles.fullContent: Sample trial: time to find the cause vs. time to first edit Minutes from the start of each run. GPT-6 Astra at max effort, Gemini 4 Carbon at high. In this sample trial, both models identified the cause early, Astra within a minute and Carbon within about six. Astra had its fix written three minutes later; Carbon didn't write any code for another 25 minutes. Carbon might not have been sure it had the cause (a knowledge gap), or it might have known and kept going anyway (a general habit, learned from training that rewards right answers more than it penalises extra steps). To tell them apart, we re-ran one of the trials in a modified harness that automatically injects the same check-in every five turns: "do you already have enough to make the fix?" Sample trial with check-ins: time to find the cause vs. time to first edit The same bug and scale as above. Gemini 4 Carbon at high, with the check-in injected every five turns (circles). With check-ins, Carbon finished in 28 minutes instead of 37, and the wait between naming the cause and editing shrank from 25 minutes to about 10. This implies that the slowness seems to come from how Carbon behaves, not what it knows.

articles.fullContent: Contents The latest Claude models were trained on protein sequences, at scale. Give Claude Fable 5.2 or Claude Opus 5.5 the start of a little-studied bacterial protein and they predict the next amino acid. Shuffle the protein and they can’t. No other model we tested can do this. Like a protein language model, they do better on bigger protein families, and they do it even in families with no papers at all. Fable 5.2 beats every open protein language model we ran, and Opus 5.5 is level with ProtGPT3-10B, the largest of them. Update, 18 November 2026. Since the first version: Proteins published after the training cutoff. With Leo Tianlai Chen, 56 proteins first made public in August 2026, with no earlier relative at 50% identity or more. The latest Claude models still predict them (Appendix G). More protein language models. ProGen3-3B is the strongest open one we ran, and Fable 5.2 still beats it; Prot-xLSTM is in Appendix C. More GPT models. GPT-6.2 Sol and Astra show no sign of it either. Motivation Frontier LLMs have started to look good at protein tasks. Atharv Jayprakash showed GPT-6 Astra ranking SOD1 variants as well as ESM-2, and PG-LLM found the same across many proteins. Did these models learn from protein sequence databases such as UniProt, or from what is written about proteins? Famous proteins can’t tell the two apart: GFP is printed in countless papers, and most frontier models recite it. So we tested proteins that almost nobody writes about. Method: next-amino-acid prediction on little-studied proteins We give a model the start of a protein and ask for the next amino acids. Then we ask again on a shuffled copy of the same protein. articles.fullContent: Google's AI answers are taking clicks from websites in the search results. In a randomized experiment, researchers hid AI Overviews from some US desktop users. Comparing them with users who still saw Overviews shows that an Overview cuts clicks to outside websites by about 40%. Those Overviews now appear on more than half the US keywords DataForSEO tracks, up from 6% two years ago. The industry's answer, GEO (generative engine optimization), has yet to show a way to compensate for the loss. While AI citations correlate with the same kind of link profile that goes with higher Google rankings, in March AI assistants sent websites just 0.3% of their traffic. Search engine optimization (SEO) still decides whether you can be found, but where an AI answer appears, a ranking brings 40% fewer visits than it used to. Generative engine optimization (GEO), the practice of getting your content cited in AI-written answers, looks mostly like SEO plus two additions: being present on the third-party sites AI answers draw from, and writing pages that are easy to quote. We found little evidence for any other tactic. Google answers first An AI Overview is a generated summary that Google places above the ordinary results, with links to the pages it drew on. In DataForSEO's monthly panel of 20 million keywords, the share of results showing one climbed from 5.93% in September 2024 to 61.43% in August 2026. The chart at the top of this post shows that climb. Over the same period the featured snippet, the quoted passage Google used to show at the top of a page, fell from 8.96% to 0.44%, and the discussions and forums block fell from 21.13% to 7.42%. Video results rose from 9.67% to 19.98%, though that is down from a peak of 31.05% in October 2025, and local map listings rose from 19.98% to 25.99%. DataForSEO's dataset covers 190 million keywords, 165 million AI answers, and 1.1 billion backlinks, mostly for US English searches. Pew Research Center's data gives an independent check. Pew logged the searches of 900 US adults in March 2025, re-ran them in April, and found summaries on 18% of them. DataForSEO's figures for those months are 14.67% and 17.63%, close to Pew's. You can't reliably avoid Overviews by choosing different keywords. Between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026, the rate rose for every type of search intent: Search intentQ4 2025Q3 2026 Informational (looking something up)48.42%70.44% Commercial (comparing options)26.30%51.35% Navigational (looking for a site)17.04%34.03% Transactional (ready to buy)10.82%28.64% Low-volume keywords aren't safer either. In the third quarter of 2026, keywords with 201 to 300 monthly searches showed Overviews 58.59% of the time, against 48.62% for those above 600. A separate dataset, from June to September 2026, covers difficulty and price. The easiest keywords showed Overviews 60.64% of the time and the hardest 53.76%. Keywords costing advertisers more than $5 a click were at 49.55% and those under 25 cents at 50.54%, with a low of 42.63% between $0.51 and $1.00. More than half the result pages have no price data and show Overviews 60.06% of the time. The rate does vary by industry. Health is at 69.68% and finance at 68.80%, while apparel is at 37.48%, dining at 29.37%, and real estate at 22.27%. Queries are also getting longer, especially on desktop. articles.fullContent: Last month, the Swiss non-profit foundation Quad9 announced that it will withdraw its free public DNS resolver from France. This difficult decision followed months of litigation and a French court ruling that imposed daily financial penalties on Quad9 for failing to block domains associated with alleged copyright infringement.Quad9’s departure from France is both disheartening and understandable. The court’s ruling put the organization in the impossible bind of having to choose between crippling litigation and penalties, or fundamentally altering its service in a way that would undermine the privacy and security of its users. Left with no good option, Quad9 is choosing the exit door instead.The withdrawal of a basic infrastructure service from France fundamentally harms the free and open Internet, and it should serve as a warning of the damage that will result if rightsholders and policymakers continue demanding maximal blocking across every layer of the Internet. It not only deprives French Internet users of a trustworthy and important tool; it creates a real risk of disruption to their daily lives. Quad9’s resolver is used by a wide variety of individuals and organizations in France — including government bodies, educational institutions, hospitals, and utilities — and Quad9 has no way to directly notify those individuals and institutions that their resolver will soon stop working. If the affected parties do not change their resolver before Quad9 removes its service, their Internet will fail with no explanation.Quad9 is not the first public DNS resolver to withdraw from a country following blocking orders, and it almost certainly won’t be the last. Cisco previously withdrew its OpenDNS resolver from France, Portugal, and Belgium (temporarily) under similar circumstances. And a Belgian court recently issued an order that would impose substantial penalties if Cloudflare, Google, and Cisco do not begin blocking websites through their public resolvers by early January 2027. That’s something Cloudflare has never done.Cloudflare has spent years advocating against orders of this kind. We are concerned that rightsholders’ unrelenting demands for blocking by public DNS resolvers will end up causing real harm to the Internet.A refresher on DNS, the Domain Name SystemTo understand why this is such a problem, it helps to understand how the Internet works under the hood. DNS resolvers are a foundational piece of the Internet’s infrastructure. DNS is the Internet’s address book: when you type a website name such as cloudflare.com, the DNS system translates that domain name into the IP address your device needs to connect to it. A DNS resolver is the service that looks up that address and sends it back to your device, much like an operator finding a phone number in a directory.DNS resolvers can be operated by anyone, but they are commonly run by Internet service providers (ISPs), mobile networks, businesses, and universities. If you’re reading this blog post at home and have never thought about DNS before, chances are that you’re using your ISP’s default resolver. Because you use your DNS resolver every time that you visit a website, it’s important for it to be reliable and trustworthy.And because the DNS resolver has access to all of your browsing activity, which resolver you use has real privacy implications.In addition to DNS resolvers that are provided by your local ISP, there are a variety of public DNS resolvers available. articles.fullContent: The Tail of Base64 By Quang Luong On affected OpenJDK builds, malformed Base64 data can cause a constant-value overwrite of allocated heap memory. Through remote Heap Feng Shui, we turn that overwrite into a heap leak and remote code execution. Discovery A few months back, I was developing a 0-click exploit on a certain phone vendor. The bug was constrained: it is a linear out-of-bounds write and we have no way to bypass ASLR. I almost considered it unexploitable until I audited the Android Runtime. Turns out, it has some predictable memory allocation pattern and if you align the registers from the starting memory corruption just right you can make the runtime interpret attacker's bytecode. After completing that exploit chain, inspired (and bored), I decided to look into some thing completely different. So I pulled the official JVM implementation (OpenJDK HotSpot) and started auditing. Java is a mature platform, so I was aware that having a "good" bug here would be hard, but I wanted to give it my best attempt anyway. Recalling my earlier lesson that complex systems and code crossing multiple boundaries are difficult to get right, I focused the audit on the JIT compiler, intrinsics, widely accessible APIs, and cryptography. Well, more precisely, I told Codex to look at those areas like any serious security researcher in 2026. To be honest, I didn't expect to find anything trivially exploitable, perhaps only some logic flaws or side-channel issues. Most early results Codex brought me were slops, either unreachable or the requirement of exploitation is not realistic at all. This looks like a gamble I am going to lose. But you know what, fortune favors the bold. So I just prompted harder... Eventually, Codex brought me a finding for a memory corruption in the Base64 decoder itself. I came looking for copper and found gold, through sheer persistence. But wait, is it really gold, or just fool's gold? The vulnerability The issue lies in OpenJDK HotSpot's x86-64 Base64 intrinsic. C2 is the most aggressive JIT compiler in the Java Virtual Machine. Specifically, if you trigger a function repeatedly, then it will compile that function into native code. Even then, ordinary native code itself is not fast enough. Modern CPUs have specialized instructions that allow processing data even faster. HotSpot uses them in optimized routines called intrinsics. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic miscalculated the padded tail's store mask, causing an out-of-bounds write. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic iterates through the input in 256-byte blocks; if it is less than 256, then it will do so in 64-byte blocks. When the input is less than 64 bytes, it uses evmovdqub, the intrinsic for the VMOVDQU8 instruction. This instruction takes a 64-bit mask that decides which bytes are read from or written to memory. The mask is first calculated from the input and output length, then updated to reflect the number of padding bytes ('=') in the Base64-encoded string. articles.fullContent: In September 1676, Ole Rømer made a prediction to the members of the Académie des Sciences in Paris. He said that on November 9, Io, one of Jupiter's moons, would emerge from the planet's shadow ten minutes later than expected. Rømer was right. In doing so, he proved that light travels at a finite speed. This knowledge became crucial to how we understand the universe today. Until then, people had believed that light travelled instantaneously from one place to another. Most viewed Regularly disappears behind Jupiter Ole Rømer was a Danish astronomer and physicist. In 1671, he travelled to Paris, where he spent ten years as a member of the scientific academy and an astronomer at the Paris Observatory, according to the Great Norwegian Encyclopedia. In the years leading up to the discovery, Rømer and other astronomers had been closely observing Io, Jupiter's third-largest moon. "Io regularly disappears behind Jupiter, and this regularity made it possible to use the moon as a clock," Jacob Wüsthoff Linder tells Science Norway.He is a professor at NTNU's Department of Physics.Such a precise ‘clock’ could be useful for navigation, among other things. Ole Eggers Bjælde, a curator at the Science Museums at Aarhus University, writes this in an article on the popular-science media outlet Videnskab.dk. Rømer studied and recorded the exact times when Io disappeared into Jupiter’s shadow and when it emerged on the other side. Discovered a patternBjælde explains that because Io orbits so close to Jupiter, only one of these events could be observed on any given night.In the days and months before Jupiter and Earth reached their closest point to each other, astronomers could observe the moon disappearing into Jupiter’s shadow. In the period after Jupiter and Earth were closest to each other, they could see Io emerging from the shadow. Rømer compiled detailed measurements of these events and eventually noticed a pattern. Rømer concluded that light took approximately 22 minutes to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit, says Professor Jacob Wüsthoff Linder. (Photo: Geir Mogen) "Rømer noticed that the eclipses occurred slightly later than expected when Earth was moving away from Jupiter, and slightly earlier when Earth was moving towards Jupiter," says Linder. "He realised that this was because the light had to travel a longer or shorter distance.""Impressive" In 1676, he therefore predicted that on November 9, Io would emerge from Jupiter's shadow ten minutes later than expected. He was correct. If light travelled instantaneously, Io should have appeared ten minutes earlier. Rømer demonstrated that light does not travel infinitely fast, says Linder. The finding was published shortly afterwards, on December 7, in Journal des sçavans. Rømer was not the first to suggest that light has a finite speed, but he is regarded as the first to demonstrate it with evidence.Other philosophers and scientists had previously theorised that light has a finite speed, including the Greek philosopher Empedocles, the Muslim scientists Ibn al-Haytham and Abu Rayhan al-Biruni, and the English philosopher and natural scientist Roger Bacon, according to Wikipedia."How accurate was Rømer's estimate of the speed of light compared with what we know today?""Not very accurate by modern standards, but impressive for 1676," says Linder.Rømer concluded that light took approximately 22 minutes to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit, says Linder. That corresponds to roughly 225,000 kilometres per second, whereas the correct value is around 300,000 kilometres per second."So his estimate was about 25 per cent too low. What really mattered, however, was not the exact figure, but that he demonstrated that the speed of light was finite and could be measured," he says. articles.fullContent: Nihilai Collective RFC8259-compliant JSON · SIMD + compile-time hash-maps · C++23 What It Is Jsonifier is a set of classes for validating, serializing, parsing, prettifying, and minifying objects into and out of JSON strings, very rapidly. It is fully RFC8259 compliant, and is positioned as possibly the fastest JSON parser and serializer in C++. It achieves this through the combined use of SIMD instructions and compile-time hash-maps for the keys of the data being parsed: so key lookup stays O(1) and order-independent rather than degrading on out-of-sequence documents. The structural index that drives every operation (parsing, serializing, minifying, prettifying) is stored as a compact array of buffer offsets rather than raw pointers, keeping the working set small and cache-friendly. Registered on the Microsoft vcpkg registry. Why Most fast JSON libraries are fast on the happy path and fragile everywhere else. Jsonifier is built to be fast and unbreakable. The serializer leans on compile-time reflection over your types, the parser resolves keys through a perfect hash computed at compile time, and the SIMD layer dispatches to the widest instruction set your CPU supports. Jsonifier doesn't just parse JSON: it survives it. Every build is hardened against malformed input: every corpus document is truncated byte by byte down to empty and each truncation must fail cleanly, and the full jsonchecker and JSONTestSuite conformance corpora are run in every parse configuration. Zero crashes, zero memory violations, zero undefined behavior : under both AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, across the full Windows / Linux / macOS matrix, on every push. Parsing, validation, minification, and prettification all fail fast now: the first invalid byte halts the operation immediately rather than letting the parser wander further into a broken buffer accumulating garbage state. Full UTF-8 validation runs as part of every parse by default, fused directly into string scanning rather than requiring a separate pass over the buffer. articles.fullContent: One Neovim, every window a real terminal pane. tmux-core.mp4 The same demo in Rex, zellij, herdr and the Herdr app. :vsplit in neopane opens a real pane in your terminal multiplexer, a Rex block, a tmux, zellij or herdr pane, and closing that pane closes the window. Neovim runs once, in the background, so every terminal attached to it shares its buffers, registers, undo and language servers. Neovim windows as real panes in Rex, tmux, zellij or herdr, with no config: pickers open as floating panes where the multiplexer has them. One editor, many terminals: neopane attach in any terminal shows the same Neovim. No multiplexer needed: in a plain terminal, it is Neovim drawn by a daemon you can attach to from other terminals and leave running. curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/spiritledsoftware/neopane/main/install.sh | bash # or: brew install spiritledsoftware/tap/neopane # or: cargo install --locked neopane neopane notes.md It needs Neovim 0.12 or later, on macOS or Linux. It is very early: bug reports are welcome on GitHub Issues. Formerly neorex. Not the original neorex by Alex Locke, which this began as and continues under that name. What it does Install Using it Pane providers Command reference Neovim arguments Environment Files and logs Troubleshooting Differences from plain Neovim Debug commands, build and tests Renamed from neorex Plans, Contributing, Sponsoring, Credits, License What it does neopane runs one Neovim in the background, a daemon, and shows it in every terminal attached to it. Buffers, registers, undo and language servers are shared by every terminal showing it. With a pane provider, each of Neovim's windows gets a terminal of its own. In Rex, :split and :vsplit open real Rex blocks where Neovim would put the window, and closing a Rex block closes its window. Focusable floats, such as pickers, open in Rex floating panes with any floats attached to them: a float group pane. A tab page opened later, as :tabnew opens one, gets a tab page area of its own, a Rex floating pane over the Rex window. The completion menu, unfocusable floats like notifications, and statuslines are drawn inside the pane they belong to. Without a pane provider, or where it can't give a window a terminal, the window is drawn in the pane it was opened from, laid out as Neovim lays out splits (ADR 0009). A tab page with no tab page area is drawn whole in the pane it opened in, and gt swaps what that pane shows, as plain Neovim swaps its screen (ADR 0012). A float group with no float group pane, as with a pane provider that has no open_float, past four float group panes, or when one fails to open, is drawn in the pane it was last entered from; while it's current and too big for that pane, Neovim's screen shrinks to the pane so the picker lays itself out to fit (ADR 0010). No pane provider is needed: in a plain terminal, neopane is Neovim drawn by a daemon, which you can attach to from other terminals, leave running, and open files in from its own :terminal. Status Very early and rough: expect bugs and missing features. neopane has been built with heavy use of AI, first in Zig and now in Rust. Much of the code still needs cleanup and better design, which is happening incrementally. Contributions are welcome: see CONTRIBUTING.md. Install You need: macOS, or Linux: it builds and passes its tests there, but hasn't been tried live yet (#43); Neovim 0.12 or later, as nvim on PATH; Rex, only for windows in Rex blocks of their own. On macOS or Linux, the latest release, as ~/.local/bin/neopane, with npane linked to it as a shorthand: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/spiritledsoftware/neopane/main/install.sh | bash Piped to NEOPANE_VERSION=v0.1.0 bash, it installs that release instead; NEOPANE_INSTALL_DIR=DIR puts it in DIR. With Homebrew, which also links npane: brew install spiritledsoftware/tap/neopane With Cargo (Rust 1.88 or later): cargo install --locked neopane Either way, a running daemon keeps the binary it started with

The walkthrough at the end follows that flow. Nothing is pushed to you, so the job polls. Its metadata is at /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server, and the protected resource metadata at /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource points to it. Register Register once with Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591): send a POST with JSON to /oauth/register. Each redirect URI is https, on any host (https://localhost included), or plain http on 127.0.0.1 or [::1]. http://localhost and custom schemes are refused with 400 invalid_redirect_uri. redirect_uris holds 1 to 32 URIs of up to 2,048 characters each. client_name is optional and up to 120 characters, and the reader sees it when approving your app. Without it, Readplace names your app after the host of the first redirect URI, without its port. There's no client secret. If you send token_endpoint_auth_method, it must be none. The 201 answer carries your client_id. Sending the same registration again returns the same client_id. A registration that never gets a token expires after 48 hours. Once it has one, it stays registered until 365 days after its latest token, refreshes included. /oauth/register and /oauth/token limit how often one IP address can call them. Over the limit, they answer 429 with a Retry-After header. Authorize Send the reader's browser to /oauth/authorize with a PKCE challenge, using S256. Readplace asks the reader to sign in if needed and to approve your app, then redirects to your redirect URI with code and state. redirect_uri must match a registered URI exactly, port included, so register the exact loopback port your app listens on. Leave out scope. Every token gets full access to the reader's account, and a refresh that sends scope is refused with 400 invalid_scope. The protected resource metadata lists that one access level in scopes_supported as account. resource is optional, because Readplace is both the authorization server and the API, so every token it issues is already for this API. articles.contentSnippet: With a team of just seven, Unsiloed AI plans to compete with tech giants and specialized startups in the crowded AI document-processing market.
articles.fullContent: As businesses increasingly turn to AI agents to automate work, the vast amounts of information locked in complex documents remain a challenge. Unsiloed AI has raised $7.5 million in seed funding led by Felicis to tackle that problem, aiming to help enterprises make their documents more accessible to AI agents through specialized technology. Silicon Valley venture capital firm Felicis led the round, with participation from Y Combinator, Orange Collective, and Uncorrelated Ventures. Angel investors Aarthi Ramamurthy and Beth Turner also participated. Business documents often include tables, charts, and complicated layouts that AI systems can struggle to interpret accurately. But getting the information wrong can lead to costly mistakes for businesses, and the impact could be severe in the case of a bank, hospital, or a law firm, as they rely on these documents for their daily work. Unsiloed aims to solve this problem with software that breaks down complex documents, extracts information from tables, charts and other elements, and turns it into structured data that AI agents can use. The technology also shows where the extracted information came from in the original document, so businesses can check the results rather than take the AI’s output at face value. “The problem with LLMs is they’re inherently probabilistic,” said Unsiloed co-founder and CEO Aman Mishra (pictured above, right) in an interview. “There is going to be some deviation induced. There is going to be some hallucination involved, and that has a massive negative impact downstream.” Mishra co-founded Unsiloed with Adnan Abbas (pictured above, left), his former classmate at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur. The two joined Y Combinator’s Fall 2025 batch after spending some time developing the technology. Unsiloed is already working with customers in finance, legal services, and healthcare, Mishra told TechCrunch. One bank is using its technology to process documents, while a law firm has deployed it on its own servers to handle contracts and old case files, he said, without naming either customer. Mishra, however, named voice AI startup Bolna AI as a customer, saying it uses Unsiloed to ingest knowledge bases for building voice agents. The San Francisco-headquartered startup has entered a market that is already crowded and includes specialized document-processing startups such as Reducto and Unstructured, as well as offerings from Microsoft and Amazon. Businesses also sometimes use general-purpose AI models to extract information from documents, giving Unsiloed another set of competitors. Mishra told TechCrunch that Unsiloed’s advantage lies in how it processes complex documents. The startup uses what it calls “dual-stream” vision models, which handle text and image data separately, along with a technique called “heat map-based chunking” that helps identify the most important parts of a document. “In one of the streams you have the text tokens, in the other stream you have the exact image tokens,” Mishra said. “This is something that we have spent a lot of time architecting.” The technology then directs more computing power toward areas such as figures, numbers, and charts. Unsiloed also uses a specialized decoder that takes industry-specific terminology into account, helping it distinguish between terms that can mean different things in different business contexts. Supporting those claims, Mishra pointed to a test involving 542 financial documents supplied by an enterprise customer. Unsiloed achieved 99.78% accuracy across roughly 84,000 extracted data points, per a technical brief shared by the startup. The test compared Unsiloed with major AI models, Microsoft’s Azure Document Intelligence, and the customer’s in-house extraction tool. The results have, however, not been independently verified. articles.title: China dominates battery graphite, but this startup could break the monopoly
articles.contentSnippet: Chinese companies maintain near total dominance of the graphite industry, but Molten Industries says its new factory in Oakland could spell the end of the monopoly.
articles.fullContent: Electric vehicle sales in the U.S. may have leveled off, but the market for batteries inside them isn’t slowing down, quintupling in the last five years. Many of those are made in the U.S., but they’re largely dependent on China for key ingredients, including graphite. Graphite is a key ingredient in lithium-ion batteries, where it forms the anode, the part that stores the battery’s charge. Chinese companies control about three-quarters of the graphite anode supply chain and 97% of synthetic (human-made) graphite anode production, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. One five-year-old startup, Molten Industries, is working to break that dominance. Molten Industries has started operating a demonstration plant in Oakland meant to prove the technology works, the company exclusively told TechCrunch. The plant is will pave the way for U.S.-made graphite to win a share of the market. “The new plant will be producing graphite that’s at cost parity with China plus tariffs,” Caleb Boyd, co-founder and CTO of Molten Industries, told TechCrunch. In other words, once U.S. import taxes are added to Chinese graphite, Molten’s price would match it. He said future plants should match China’s cost even without tariffs, which he called a built-in advantage of the technology. Molten’s Oakland plant will make about 300 metric tons of graphite annually, which is enough for 300 megawatt-hours of batteries. That’s enough for about 4,300 EVs. The bulk of the output will go to undisclosed customers that are testing it in their battery cells. The next facility, which Molten has yet to announce, will take the same template used in the Oakland plant and replicate it several times over, said Boyd. The startup’s technology began in a Silicon Valley garage. It uses electrical resistive heating, which passes electricity through a material to heat it, to split methane (the main ingredient in natural gas) into pure carbon and hydrogen. “You can think of it almost like a massive toaster,” Boyd said. The company says the system uses three times less electricity than existing methods, and it runs on natural gas, which is cheap and plentiful in the U.S. “We think it’s very hard to compete with China if you’re just copying their processes and trying to compete on cost,” said Kevin Bush, who co-founded Molten Industries with Boyd and is the company’s CEO. “So we are using a resource in the United States that’s abundant in natural gas, and we’ve brought some innovation to actually be able to drive down the cost of graphite production globally.” Here’s how the chemistry works: When methane (CH4) is heated without oxygen, each molecule breaks into one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. The hydrogen atoms pair up into hydrogen gas (H2), which Molten sells at market prices to a customer next door. The carbon is then processed to meet battery makers’ requirements. The basic idea of using heat to separate methane has been around for over a century, but early attempts to commercialize it ran into trouble. Carbon built up and clogged the reactor, and Boyd said no company before Molten had been able to produce high-quality graphite this way. Solving that problem changed the company’s direction. Boyd and Bush — both materials science PhDs from Stanford — originally set out to make clean hydrogen from natural gas. Most hydrogen today comes from steam reforming, a cheap but polluting process. The two wanted to reap the benefits of a low-cost feedstock like natural gas without the pollution, and they expected to sell the leftover carbon as a byproduct. But as they experimented with ways to keep the reactor clean, “we actually started making this really high quality graphite,” Boyd said, which “changed the entire economics of what we were doing.” Molten went from a hydrogen company that happened to sell graphite to a battery-grade graphite company that happens to sell hydrogen. articles.title: Nvidia’s startup stakes ballooned to $65B, but Huang’s exit puts future  deals in doubt
articles.contentSnippet: The value of Nvidia’s private investments has nearly tripled over the past nine months, fueled by Jensen Huang’s aggressive dealmaking and rising valuations of its existing portfolio companies.
articles.fullContent: Nvidia’s equity in private companies continues to grow: it revealed its stakes are now worth $65.5 billion on Tuesday, up from the $22 billion reported in January. The increase includes both new investments and significant markups of existing portfolio companies. The company invested $16 billion into equities in the past quarter alone, it said, and $58 billion in the past nine months of its fiscal year. This amount includes buying shares in public and private companies, yet it shows how the chipmaker made massive bets over the course of the year, especially compared to last year; in November 2025, the company reported spending $5 billion buying equity in the first nine months of that fiscal year. But it’s unclear if this growth will continue under the interim CEO and Jensen Huang’s successor. Nvidia stated in late 2023 that the goal of its corporate investing is to expand the AI ecosystem by backing startups it considers to be “game changers and market makers.” Over the nearly three years that followed, the chipmaker has invested in nearly 350 startups, according to PitchBook. The companies Nvidia backed include Anthropic, OpenAI; neolabs like Thinking Machines and Reflection; neoclouds, like Lambda, Nscale, and Crusoe; as well as other companies developing AI infrastructure, robotics startups, and applications. It’s also become a big financier of the data center build out, reporting $118 billion in guarantees with $105 billion of that the backstop it supplied for OpenAI’s $500 billion data center in Ohio. The company made those commitments by allocating a meaningful portion of its excess cash flows. In Tuesday’s earning call, Kress said Nvidia would continue providing financing assistance to strong customers and that “as the market matures and additional sources of capital become available,” the company would be “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.” But the question for the VC ecosystem is whether the company will continue to back startups at anywhere near the same level without Huang at the helm. Huang’s rampant dealmaking has reportedly been a source of concern for Kress. Investors have told TechCrunch that they anticipate that she will take a more conservative approach to startup investing, becoming more selective with new investments and writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio companies. “We intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders during this last quarter and going forward,” Kress said on the earnings call on Tuesday. Just how strategic startups will be under her leadership, and under the future permanent CEO, remains to be seen. But for now, VCs are bracing for a meaningful pullback in capital. articles.title: Stripe backer Atomico calls for Europe to own its success stories
articles.contentSnippet: Europe is home to many of the world's fastest growing companies of all time, veteran VC firm Atomico highlighted in its latest annual State of European Tech report.
articles.fullContent: Europe is home to many of the world’s fastest growing companies of all time, veteran VC firm Atomico highlighted in its latest annual State of European Tech report. The report, for instance, notes that the likes of Black Forest Labs and Microagi have reached $100 million in revenue in months, not years. “I think we can put to bed the idea that there’s a fundamental reason or constraint on the ability to scale a breakout company from here in Europe,” Atomico partner and head of intelligence Tom Wehmeier (pictured) told TechCrunch. Yet, there’s still more that the VC firm founded by Skype’s Niklas Zennström would like to see — and its call this year is for Europe to “build it” and “scale it,” but also “own it.” That’s a way of wishing these companies will remain European longer. But there’s also a sense that this success hasn’t been acknowledged enough, perhaps obscured by louder calls for improvements. Wehmeier, the report’s lead author, was quick to opine that “policy, procurement and capital are not moving at the same speed as our founders.” But he said the tech sector should advocate for itself in an inspiring way. “When it comes to policy, I think the language needs to be, ‘Hey, this is not us complaining. This is us saying here is an opportunity to make the magnitude of impact even greater,’” Wehmeier said. “When we frame it as problems, that becomes harder.” This reframing may also help European tech improve its image abroad, where complaints around overregulation may have overshadowed Europe’s potential to leverage its deep tech talent and growing pool of repeat entrepreneurs to have even more of success stories. Image Credits:Atomico Plenty could be still done to fully unlock this potential, and Wehmeier said that “the next few weeks are going to be a really important test, with EU Inc.” Also known as the 28th regime, this initiative would create a unified European corporate regime akin to the Delaware C Corp. If the last stretch of EU Inc’s grassroots campaign achieves it goal, it will become much easier to create and operate businesses across the EU. It would also show that the tech system got itself heard, which could open the door to the kind of endorsement Atomico is hoping to see more of. Politicians have strong incentives to give the tech sector what it wants. If it is Europe’s second largest sector, biggest contributor to growth, and biggest job creator, “Do we not want more of that?” Wehmeier asked rhetorically. But it is unclear whether it will win them any votes. To make the answer more straightforward, the tech sector will have to work on having public opinion on its side. For Wehmeier, one key is to “demonstrate that this is translating into value for citizens.” The report is supporting this endeavor with a mix of high-level data and examples from its portfolio; for instance, it notes that ICEYE’s satellites monitor severe weather, flooding, and other hazards; and Daniel Ek’s Neko Health has now done more than 100,000 body scans, some of which helped identify severe or life-threatening health conditions. One limit to this argument is that Neko Health’s scans will seem pricey to most Europeans, who largely rely on collective, public health insurance. articles.title: Nvidia is abandoning China after Jensen Huang’s ouster
articles.contentSnippet: Nvidia's interim CEO says the company is done selling chips to China. How much will that cost?
articles.fullContent: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country. China’s access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the company’s first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia announced it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks. Nvidia’s deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff. The pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States’ lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more important for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that “to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country.” Huang’s ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely. Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia’s data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress said that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company’s top-line revenue. In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Critics of Nvidia’s dependence on China claim that as much as 20% of its revenue comes from demand linked to the country — annual revenue at its Singapore subsidiary hit $104 billion in 2025 before Nvidia stopped disclosing those figures — but that’s clearly going to change. Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country’s domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute users want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Feldgoise, a researcher at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. Meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China’s leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China. That training may have taken place at data centers outside of China, but sales to those facilities will be barred under the new rules. If large data centers suited for training AI models want to buy Nvidia chips, they will have to certify they aren’t serving any Chinese customers, export control attorney Dan Fisher-Owens told TechCrunch. If they can’t provide that certification, the new rules may force them toward other chip options and further eat into Nvidia’s market share. articles.title: Nvidia says its open source AI strategy remains intact after Jensen Huang’s exit
articles.contentSnippet: Nvidia's interim CEO reaffirmed its open source AI strategy and plans to acquire Hugging Face, despite Jensen Huang's sudden departure.
articles.fullContent: Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress reaffirmed the company’s commitment to open source AI during Tuesday’s earnings call with analysts — the first since CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation. “At Nvidia, we are committed to fostering a vibrant open model ecosystem, so every country, company, and industry can build its own intelligence,” Kress said in her opening remarks. She also noted that open models were accelerating AI adoption, citing a 35-fold year-over-year surge in weekly token volume on OpenRouter, including a 3.5-fold increase over the past three months. Kress also spoke about Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face, a platform for open source AI models that the company agreed to acquire for $12.9 billion in September, in what would be the second-largest acquisition in Nvidia’s history. The platform, which serves more than 18 million developers and 200,000 companies, is still on track to join Nvidia, despite Huang’s ouster. Huang had heavily advocated for open source AI technology. His departure had raised questions about the company’s future approach to open source AI models, with Hugging Face’s CEO calling Huang’s departure “a sad day,” and promising to “keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever.” So far, Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face appear unchanged. The acquisition was not directly addressed during the Q&A portion of the earnings call. “Together, we will scale its platform and make intelligence more open, more capable, and more accessible,” said Kress of Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face. Last week, Nvidia founder Huang resigned from his position as CEO following news about his extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. He’s also accused of having extramarital affairs with two direct reports and is now set to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving. Meanwhile, the SEC is investigating Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors, The WSJ reported. Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads. On today’s call, Kress noted that Nemotron is now the “most widely used U.S. open model on OpenRouter,” and it’s “where developers start to build their own intelligence.” “That foundation is empowering the ecosystem,” she said. articles.title: Nvidia says it doesn’t plan to reappoint Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.contentSnippet: The former CEO offered to return to his top role at the company after his resignation last week.
articles.fullContent: Despite Nvidia founder and former CEO Jensen Huang’s recent offer to return to the chip company he helped build from the ground up, the company is not looking to take him back. During the company’s earnings call on Tuesday, Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones told listeners that Huang’s return was not something that company leadership was considering. “On November 12, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms,” Jones said, “Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO, and board member. The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” On Tuesday, Huang had posted on X that since he left the company, he has “seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” and added that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Huang resigned last week in dramatic fashion following revelations of a number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman who has been accused of being a Chinese intelligence agent. That woman, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, has maintained close ties to the former Nvidia CEO for years. Critics worry that the relationship may have influenced Nvidia’s dealings with China, and U.S. intelligence officials have expressed suspicions that she works for China’s Ministry of State Security. The development has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry at a moment when the future of the AI business, in which Nvidia plays a pivotal role, hangs in the balance. It has also spurred investigations, including an independent investigation into Huang’s activities by Nvidia’s board and an SEC probe into Nvidia. Huang has been replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress, who is also the chipmaker’s chief financial officer and executive vice president, while the board searches for a permanent replacement. articles.title: Amazon and Google will together own nearly 30% of Anthropic after its IPO
articles.contentSnippet: Amazon will own just under 15% of Anthropic after the IPO, with the option to go much higher. Google is a close second with holdings of nearly 14%.
articles.fullContent: Anthropic on Tuesday disclosed more details about the biggest investment agreements with major cloud providers Amazon and Google. While we already knew that Amazon stood to make a killing on its Anthropic investments from the IPO, Anthropic revealed that Amazon’s total stake will come in at just shy of 15% (14.7% to be exact). Even more interesting is that Amazon could have, if it wished, owned an even bigger share of the company. When Amazon invested billions in Anthropic in 2023 and 2024 (long before Claude Code took the enterprise world by storm, back in the days when Anthropic looked like it would forever be a speck in OpenAI’s shadow), the cloud giant obtained promissory notes that could convert into equity. These notes carry conversion prices of about $2.09 or $5.05 per share, depending on the year of investment. Amazon has opted to convert a chunk of them as part of the IPO into a special class of non-voting shares that will give it about 15% ownership. (The shares can receive dividends and convert to standard voting Class A shares when sold, the filing says.) But it has also opted to hold on to billions of dollars’ worth of the notes for now. If it converted them all right now, it would own just under 24% of Anthropic (23.8% to be precise). Google, meanwhile, will own just under 14% (13.7%), also in non-voting shares, which come from the conversion of notes, as well as the “private placement” sale of shares as part of this IPO. A group of major tech companies (AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC Partners) have agreed to buy $26 billion worth of this non-voting stock. Google and Nvidia each agreed to buy $10 billion worth. So while a lot of investors stand to make billions of dollars in Anthropic’s IPO, Amazon is one of the biggest winners, and that doesn’t even count what AWS stands to earn from Anthropic’s commitment to spend more than $100 billion on its cloud services over the next decade. articles.fullContent: In Brief Posted: 1:48 PM PST · November 17, 2026 Image Credits:Tomohiro Ohsumi / Getty Images The Securities and Exchange Commission is opening a civil probe into Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors, according to The Wall Street Journal. The investigation adds to Nvidia’s stack of drama after CEO Jensen Huang resigned following news of his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based data company Megaspeed. The Commerce Department has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024 under suspicion that the company diverted some of its Nvidia chips to China, which would violate U.S. export laws. Congress has also demanded that Huang answer questions about his affair and how it might have affected his stance that export restrictions should be loosened. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent put it more bluntly over the weekend, accusing Nvidia of knowingly selling powerful chips to China to “goose their revenues and their earnings.” The news of the SEC probe also comes as Nvidia reports earnings to a market that has seen its stock fall more than 10% since Huang departed. articles.title: Google joins the tech outage trend by announcing it’s not having one
articles.contentSnippet: With tech outages seemingly everywhere, Google took the unusual step of announcing that Gmail is working just fine, actually.
articles.fullContent: Was Google feeling a little left out of the recent wave of tech outages? The company took to X on Tuesday to announce that its Gmail service is actually running just fine. In a post, the company said it was not currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption and reminded users they could always check Gmail’s real-time status on its online dashboard. As it turns out, the company was trying to head off reports of a Gmail outage that began circulating on X on Tuesday around the same time that Apple was seeing a number of verified outages of its own. While some posts on the social network suggested Gmail was experiencing a disruption, others said they were not having any problems. The concerns seemed to stem from an X post by Downdetector, a crowdsourced website where users can report service disruptions themselves and see if others are having problems. Downdetector is not an official source for verifying or understanding the true scope of internet outages, and as people become more concerned about possible cyberattacks, the site’s data may become less valuable over time if every minor glitch and hiccup is reported as an “outage” by non-technical users. The fact that Google had to announce it was not having an outage speaks to the growing anxiety around the reliability of major tech services. Over the past week, Apple and Microsoft experienced outages, an FAA network failure led to a nationwide ground stop, and some banks and airlines also reported disruptions. However, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Fox Business Network’s “The Claman Countdown” on Tuesday that the U.S. is not currently facing coordinated cyberattacks. He told the outlet, “We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack — let me just be clear about that — and we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here.” Instead, Clayton attributed the rise in issues to businesses patching their systems. The patching may be a downstream effect of AI, as newer models have become increasingly adept at uncovering previously unknown vulnerabilities. “They’re upgrading them, they’re putting patches in place,” he said, adding that this is happening at “a much larger scale” than before. articles.title: Waymo suspends freeway rides nationwide after California DMV order
articles.contentSnippet: The DMV said Waymo's freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety.  Restrictions will remain in place until Waymo can demonstrate that it has taken "effective corrective actions" to address the deficiencies.
articles.fullContent: Waymo robotaxis are no longer allowed to operate on California freeways after the state’s Department of Motor Vehicles restricted the Alphabet-owned company’s operations following several incidents that raised safety concerns. California’s DMV, which regulates the testing and deployment of autonomous vehicles in the state, issued the operational restrictions on Waymo on November 11. However, the restrictions weren’t made public until Tuesday. San Francisco Business Times was the first to report the order. The DMV confirmed the new restrictions to TechCrunch, stating that the department took action after three Waymo autonomous vehicles entered an active construction closure on U.S. Route 101 near Burlingame, and another separate incident involving California Highway Patrol vehicles on Highway 280 in San Francisco. Waymo has complied and is preventing its robotaxis from accessing freeways in any of the markets it operates in, including those outside of California. Waymo currently has commercial operations in 15 U.S. cities. The DMV said Waymo’s freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety. “The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present, despite a prior restriction and corrective actions implemented following similar incidents that occurred on May 18, 2026,” according to an emailed statement sent to TechCrunch. The DMV said the restrictions will remain in place until Waymo can demonstrate that it has taken “effective corrective actions” to address the deficiencies. Waymo spokesperson Dana Gallagher told TechCrunch the company has temporarily restricted freeway operations across its other operating markets to evaluate its performance. “Safety is at the foundation of everything we do,” Gallagher said in a statement. “Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.” Waymo began offering freeway rides in late 2025, a commercial milestone that has been central to its expansion in major metro areas. Freeway access allows Waymo to connect riders to airports and other destinations more efficiently, slashing travel times by avoiding slower surface streets. That has been particularly important in the San Francisco Bay Area because Waymo’s service area stretches from the city south to Silicon Valley. Freeway access has dramatically shortened trips across the Peninsula that previously took 45 minutes or more than an hour. In May, Waymo abruptly stopped operating on highways. The company didn’t cite a specific reason at the time, but several social media posts showed Waymo robotaxis driving through traffic cones and struggling to navigate construction zones. Waymo robotaxis returned to freeways in July after the company said it updated the self-driving software system to improve performance around freeway construction zones. articles.contentSnippet: The startup says its agents understand the full context of deals that bankers and consultants are working on and can automatically update financial models and presentations when new developments affect their analysis.
articles.fullContent: In Brief Posted: 11:32 AM PST · November 17, 2026 Image Credits:shapecharge / Getty Images Model ML, a London-based startup that uses AI to automate work traditionally performed by junior bankers and consultants, including building financial models, preparing pitch decks, and writing due diligence reports, has raised $250 million in Series B funding at a $1.5 billion valuation. The new round, which comes a year after its $75 million Series A round was announced, was co-led by General Atlantic and earlier backer QED Investors. Brothers Chaz and Arnie Englander co-founded the three-year-old startup after previously co-founding two other companies, including Fat Llama, a peer-to-peer rental marketplace acquired by Swedish rival Hygglo for $41.5 million in 2022. Model ML develops AI agents that integrate with clients’ systems, data, and tools, including Excel and PowerPoint. The startup says its agents understand the full context of deals that bankers and consultants are working on and can automatically update financial models and presentations when new developments affect their analysis. Other startups automating the routine, repetitive tasks for investment bankers and management consultants include Hebbia and Rogo, which raised $160 million at a $2 billion valuation in April. Anthropic and OpenAI have also built tools for financial professionals, but Model ML says it runs on open source models and that doing so allows it to operate at about 2% of the cost of frontier models while delivering faster results. articles.title: Google expands access to Gemini Tasks, which can help with calls, purchases
articles.contentSnippet: Gemini's Task mode can help users coordinate calls, log into websites, and even make purchases on the user's behalf.
articles.fullContent: In Brief Posted: 11:02 AM PST · November 17, 2026 Image Credits:Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto / Getty Images Google is expanding the rollout of Tasks, a toggle in Gemini that converts the chatbot into a more active helper. Unlike Gemini’s Chat, which merely allows users to talk to Google’s AI assistant for informational purposes, Tasks empowers the app to complete basic secretarial functions, deputizing it as a kind of personal assistant. How, specifically, can you use it? Google says that the app can call businesses and book appointments on users’ behalf; it can also complete purchases for them via Google Pay, and even sign into websites securely if prompted to do so. In a blog post, Josh Woodword, VP of Gemini, claims to have recently used the feature to call local car dealerships to schedule a service appointment for his family’s minivan. He says he also used it to analyze his electrical bill. Tasks was initially launched to select testers back in May as Gemini Spark, a 24/7 agentic helper, and was expanded to U.S. subscribers of its Google AI Ultra tier. Gemini Spark eventually became “Task Mode.” Google is now making the feature available for free to hundreds of millions of people who are using the company’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. Getting the function up and running is easy. Users merely flip a toggle within the app from Chat to Tasks, which enables the feature. Users can also send texts to Gemini or call the app to give it commands. Newsletters Subscribe for the industry’s biggest tech news Related Latest in AI

articles.title: Apple services, including iCloud, App Store, Apple Music, and more, hit by outage
articles.contentSnippet: Apple's status page confirms its services are facing outages, but has not confirmed the cause.
articles.fullContent: After a recent slew of tech outages, service disruptions, and flight chaos this week, it’s now Apple customers who are facing technical issues. The iPhone maker’s System Status page indicates that there are issues with iCloud’s Account & Sign In services affecting “all users,” which could make the service slow or unavailable. The App Store, AppleCare on Device, and Apple Music are also experiencing issues, the page indicates. Like all major tech companies, Apple faces outages and other technical issues affecting its cloud services at times. However, today’s issues are likely more noticeable to end users because problems with iCloud can lead to account sign-in problems. This could cause your iPhone to ask for your Apple ID and password, and you could see other attempts to sign in to services with your Apple account information fail. On Reddit, some folks also noted that they were unable to activate a new iPhone, which is likely related to these ongoing issues. Given the recent increase in AI-driven cyberattacks, users across social media have already begun to speculate about the cause. In particular, users are expressing concerns about the Apple outage, as it arrives only days after technical failures at Microsoft led to its cloud systems that power flagship services like Outlook and Teams failing due to cascading software issues. Similarly, a brief outage of Chase’s banking app this week garnered attention, as did an ongoing partial outage (at the time of publication) of the National Security Agency’s internal classified network, both of which were blamed on software glitches. So far, none of the outages in the past week have been attributed to cyberattacks, but rather to technical problems. Apple responded to TechCrunch’s request for comment (which it initially gave to Bloomberg), noting that the outages were caused by an internal update and not a cyberattack. “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” the statement read. After the initial outages were reported, Apple’s status page was updated to include other outages impacting Apple School Manager, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps (iCloud.com), Schoolwork, and the Volume Purchase Program. By 6 PM ET on Tuesday, the status page showed all the outages were resolved. This article was updated after publication with the status of the outages. articles.title: Google to keep Gemini chats for 2 months, up from 72 hours, even with history off
articles.contentSnippet: Google's Gemini update extending chat retention will roll out globally over the coming weeks.
articles.fullContent: Image Credits:Jagmeet Singh / TechCrunch 10:48 AM PST · November 17, 2026 Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable. The change, which will roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks, marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period mentioned in Google’s Gemini Apps Privacy Hub, according to an archived version from November 12. OpenAI, by comparison, says it may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default. However, companies may keep some data longer for legal or safety reasons, or to investigate policy violations. Google did not answer questions about what prompted the change and whether it would affect how conversations are accessed or reviewed, instead pointing to a blog post that says chats are kept longer to respond to users, process feedback, and protect its services and users. Its updated Gemini Apps Privacy Hub also cites potential system failures as a reason for retaining chats and says temporary conversations are not used to train AI models. The longer retention period comes as Google introduces separate settings for Gemini’s chat history and AI training. Until now, both were tied to a single “Keep Activity” setting. Users will now be able to keep their conversations in their chat history without using them to train Google’s generative AI models. Google says both new settings will be turned off by default for users who previously disabled Keep Activity. For those who had Keep Activity turned on, their chat history will remain enabled. They can, though, decide separately whether Google can use their conversations to train AI models. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission.
